text: Every year, Americans make about a hundred and fifty-five million emergency visits, and every one of them sets off a chain of work.
Before the visit, there are referrals to read, insurers to call, and appointments to find.
During the visit there are hallways and waiting rooms, and afterwards there are results and phone calls that nobody returns.
Each link in that chain belongs to a different person, and nobody holds the whole line.
Those gaps are expensive, because about a quarter of US health spending is estimated to be waste.
Doctors and their staff lose around thirteen hours a week to prior authorization alone.
And one abnormal test result in fourteen never reaches the patient at all.
[MUSIC HIT - no VO]
Take Maria, who is seventy-one and whose doctor has just found something on a scan.
Dr. Whitcombe refers her to Halden Medical Center the way most offices still do, by fax.
That fax is where Throughline picks up the thread.
Thirteen agents pass Maria's case from one to the next, and people sign off at the moments that matter.
The Intake agent reads the fax, and when it can't make out the member number, it asks the coordinator instead of guessing.
That one answer wakes up Coverage, which sees that the scan needs approval and hands it to Prior auth.
Prior auth drafts the whole request and shows the source of every line.
The coordinator only has to read it and approve, instead of spending twenty-four minutes writing it by hand.
Scheduling then fits every appointment into as few trips as possible, using an exact engine written in Rust.
Visit prep sends Maria her plan, and when she replies with a voice note about a wheelchair, Messaging understands it and Itinerary routes her around the stairs.
[MUSIC HIT - no VO]
On the day of her visit, one of the two CT scanners breaks down, and nobody raises the alarm.
The waiting-room agent counts the people in the camera frames and sees the line growing.
It passes the problem straight to the Ops planner.
The planner plays out the next ninety minutes twenty times to compare every fix it knows.
The best option brings the average CT wait down from seventeen minutes to five.
The operations lead approves it, seven patients are re-planned, and the Visit companion tells each of them what changed and why.
When Maria gets home, the Discharge agent puts the doctor's notes into plain words, and the doctor signs off.
If she is still unsure the next day, Discharge hands her to a nurse.
Results watch makes sure her test is acknowledged, and Follow-up books her next visit to close the loop.
The agents that read, write, and listen run on Muse Spark and Voice Transcribe, and SAM does the counting.
The Ops planner runs on Muse Spark Open, an open-weights model hosted on Baseten.
And it is built for more than one hospital, because Northgate alone has five buildings and a fourteen-floor tower.
[MUSIC HIT - no VO]
Nobody had to hold Maria's thread by hand.
This time, Throughline held it for her.
